meta.title: Your First Mortgage Payment Barely Touches The Loan. Here's Why.
meta.hook: In the first years of a 30-year mortgage, most of your payment isn't paying down the loan at all.
meta.description: Mortgages use amortization schedules that front-load interest: in the early years, the majority of each fixed payment covers interest on the full remaining balance, with only a small slice reducing principal. Over time that ratio flips, and later payments knock down principal much faster. It's a structural feature of how the loan is repaid, not a hidden fee.

scenes.narration: In the first years of a thirty-year mortgage, most of your payment isn't paying down the loan at all.

scenes.narration: It's mostly going toward interest, on the full amount you still owe.

scenes.narration: That's how amortization works. Every fixed payment is split between interest and principal, and early on, interest wins that split.

scenes.narration: As the balance shrinks, less interest is owed each month, so more of the same payment starts chipping away at principal.

scenes.narration: By the back half of the loan, the split flips almost completely, and most of the payment finally builds equity.
